body.heading: The simplest game there is
paragraphs: Tag needs no equipment, no pitch and no explanation: one player is “it”, and if they touch you, you are it. Variants of chasing-and-touching games appear in cultures across the world and deep into history — it may be the oldest game format humans have.

Its endless variations are local inventions. Freeze tag turns tagged players into statues until a teammate's touch frees them. Shadow tag is played by stepping on shadows, which makes it a game of sunshine and angles. TV tag lets you dodge a tag by crouching and naming a show — no repeats allowed.

body.heading: Kho kho: tag as a team sport
paragraphs: India's kho kho takes tag to another level entirely. A chasing team sits in a line, alternating the way they face; only one chaser is active at a time, and they can tag a seated teammate — shouting “kho!” — to hand over the chase in a new direction. Three defenders dodge, dive and double back against the whole relay.
Kho kho is one of India's oldest traditional games and is now played in organised leagues — proof that a playground chase, refined over centuries, becomes a sport of split-second strategy.

body.heading: Try it: invent your local variant
paragraphs: Start a family tournament of classic tag, then let each player add one rule for the next round: a safe base, a hopping-only zone, a statue rescue. Write the winning rules down — you are doing what playgrounds have done for a thousand years.

If you have nine or more players and some space, try a gentle kho kho: seat the chasers in a line and let them pass the chase with a shout. The first time the relay cuts off a runner's escape, you will feel the genius of it.

takeaway: Tag is humanity's default game — and each culture that touches it leaves a new rule, a new name and a better chase.
